lessons.title: China 2015: The Stock Market Bust and the Yuan Shock

body.text: A government can pump up a stock market and freeze trading when it falls, but it cannot stop money from leaving the country. In 2015, China learnt that controlling prices is not the same as controlling confidence.

children.text: On 11 August 2015, the People's Bank of China cut the yuan's daily reference rate against the dollar by 1.9%. It sounds small. It was the largest one-day move in two decades, and it came from a central bank that markets believed would always keep the yuan steady. Two months earlier, China's stock market had begun collapsing from a borrowed-money bubble. Together, the two shocks sent capital rushing out of China and markets tumbling worldwide, including on Dalal Street.

This chapter turns to the world's second largest economy. This first lesson covers the 2015 crisis, which exposed the limits of a state-managed financial system and set the stage for the property and debt problems in the next two lessons.

children.text: Build-up: A Bull Market on Borrowed Money

Between July 2014 and June 2015, the Shanghai Composite index rose from about 2,050 to 5,166. China's economy was slowing, but state media encouraged ordinary citizens to invest, and many saw the government's backing as a guarantee that prices would keep rising.
Much of the buying was done with borrowed money.
Margin financing
on the Shanghai and Shenzhen exchanges hit a record 2.27 trillion yuan on 18 June 2015, and estimates of unregulated grey-market lending ran to trillions more.

markDefs.definition: Borrowing money from a broker to buy shares, using the shares themselves as collateral. It magnifies gains and losses, and if prices fall far enough, the broker demands more cash or sells the shares.

body.title: What a 43% Fall Does to a Margin Investor
body.prompt: A Chinese investor buys ¥100,000 of shares using ¥50,000 of their own money and ¥50,000 borrowed from a broker. The shares then fall 43%, the same as the index from June to August 2015. What percentage of their own money has the investor lost, ignoring interest and fees?
body.explanation: The shares are now worth ¥100,000 × 57% = ¥57,000. The investor still owes the broker ¥50,000, so their own stake is ¥57,000 minus ¥50,000 = ¥7,000. They started with ¥50,000, so they have lost ¥43,000, or 86%. With just 2 to 1 leverage, a 43% market fall wipes out 86% of the investor's money. In reality, most brokers would have sold them out long before that.

body.text: Margin lending turns a falling market into a crashing one. When prices drop, brokers issue margin calls. Investors who cannot pay are sold out automatically, and those forced sales push prices down further, triggering more margin calls. This is the same fire sale spiral you saw with repo haircuts in 2008.

children.text: Panic: The Crash and the Rescue

The market peaked on 12 June 2015 and then fell hard, losing about a third of its value in three weeks as regulators tried to rein in margin lending. Beijing responded with a rescue unlike anything in a major market.

events.title: The peak
events.description: The Shanghai Composite closes at 5,166, about 150% above its level a year earlier.

events.title: Margin debt peaks
events.description: Formal margin loans reach a record 2.27 trillion yuan.

events.title: The national team moves in
events.description: State-backed institutions start buying more than 1,000 stocks, and planned IPOs are halted.

events.title: The market freezes
events.description: Major shareholders are banned from selling for six months. By 9 July, 1,476 companies, more than half of all listed firms, have suspended trading.

events.title: The yuan shock
events.description: The central bank cuts the yuan's reference rate by 1.9%, the largest one-day move in two decades.

events.title: Black Monday
events.description: The Shanghai index falls 8.5%. The Sensex falls 1,624 points, and markets drop worldwide.

events.title: The low of the first crash
events.description: The index is 43% below its June peak, and margin loans have shrunk to about 1.25 trillion yuan.

events.title: The circuit breaker fiasco
events.description: A new market-wide circuit breaker halts trading on 4 and 7 January and is scrapped after four days.

body.title: How markets normally handle a crash vs China's 2015 response

Trading stays open so investors can exit

body.text: Suspending trading did not remove the losses. It trapped investors inside them. An investor holding a suspended stock could not sell, so they sold whatever they still could, spreading the pressure to the shares that remained open. Liquidity that disappears exactly when you need it is not liquidity.

children.text: The Yuan Shock and the Flight of Capital

China's currency was tightly managed. Each day, the central bank set a reference rate, and the yuan could only trade within a band around it. For years, markets treated the yuan as a one-way bet that would hold steady or rise. The 1.9% cut on 11 August 2015 broke that belief.

Chinese companies and households that had borrowed in dollars rushed to repay, and many savers tried to move money abroad before the yuan fell further. To stop the currency collapsing, the central bank sold dollars from its reserves on an enormous scale. China's reserves, which had peaked at $3.99 trillion in June 2014, fell below $3 trillion in January 2017, a drop of about a quarter. In 2016 alone, China used nearly $320 billion of reserves, and the yuan still fell 6.6% that year.

body.title: Why Burn a Trillion Dollars?
body.question: Chapter 4 introduced the impossible trinity. In 2015 and 2016, China wanted a stable yuan and independent interest rates. What did it have to do to achieve both?
options: Raise interest rates sharply to match the US Federal Reserve
Let the yuan float freely with no intervention
Restrict money leaving the country, after first spending huge reserves while those restrictions were loose
Join a currency union with its trading partners
body.explanation: Under the impossible trinity, a country can have only two of: a stable exchange rate, independent interest rates and free capital movement. China wanted the first two, so capital movement had to give. While money was still leaking out, the central bank spent reserves to hold the yuan up. It then tightened capital controls, checking conversions of yuan into foreign currency and scrutinising overseas investments, and by early 2017 reserves had begun to recover.

children.text: How It Reached India

body.label: Black Monday on Dalal Street
body.context: A fall of 5.94%, then the Sensex's biggest single-day point drop, wiping out over ₹7 lakh crore of investor wealth. The rupee weakened to 66.69 per dollar as global investors fled emerging markets.

children.text: India had little direct exposure to Chinese shares, so the damage came through the wake-up call and capital flight channels from Chapter 1. Investors worried that a weaker yuan would make Chinese exports cheaper, hurting competitors like India, and that a slowing China would cut global demand for commodities. They sold emerging markets across the board and asked questions later.

body.title: Go deeper: why China's circuit breaker made panic worse

children.text: In January 2016, China introduced a market-wide circuit breaker that halted trading for 15 minutes if the CSI 300 index fell 5%, and for the rest of the day if it fell 7%. The gap between the two levels was narrow.
Once the index fell close to 5%, investors feared being locked in during a halt.
They rushed to sell before trading stopped, pushing the index down faster.
After the 15-minute pause, the same fear returned, now aimed at the 7% level.
The market hit 7% quickly on 4 January and again within half an hour of opening on 7 January.

This is sometimes called the magnet effect: a trading halt that is too close pulls prices towards it. India's market-wide circuit breakers, triggered by index moves of 10%, 15% and 20%, give far more room before trading stops, which reduces that pull.

body.title: Name the Demand
body.textWithBlank: When the value of shares bought with borrowed money falls too far, the broker demands more cash from the investor. This demand is called a margin ___.
body.explanation: A margin call. If the investor cannot add cash, the broker sells the shares, and millions of forced sales at once are what turned China's 2015 correction into a crash.

body.title: Lessons for India's Retail Trading Boom
body.scenario: India has seen its own surge of new retail participants in markets, especially in futures and options. A SEBI study published in September 2024 found that 93% of individual equity F&O traders lost money between 2021-22 and 2023-24, with aggregate losses of more than ₹1.8 lakh crore. A friend argues that India is nothing like China in 2015, because the Indian government does not tell people to buy shares.
body.prompt: Where is your friend right, where might the comparison still hold, and what lessons from China 2015 would you apply to your own investing?
body.modelAnswer: Where the friend is right: India's rise in participation was not driven by state media urging people to buy, SEBI has tightened rules on F&O trading rather than encouraging it, India's markets did not suspend half of all listed companies in a fall, and the rupee is not managed through a tightly controlled daily reference rate the way the yuan was in 2015. Where the comparison still holds: leverage. F&O positions and margin trading facilities give traders exposure far larger than their capital, just as margin loans did in China, so a sharp market move can wipe out traders quickly and force selling. A wave of new, inexperienced participants who have only seen rising markets is also a common feature of both. The SEBI finding that 93% of individual F&O traders lost money shows that leverage in inexperienced hands tends to transfer wealth rather than create it. Lessons to apply: know exactly how much leverage you are using and what move would wipe out your capital; do not assume a market will keep rising because it has risen recently or because authorities seem supportive; keep positions small enough that you are never forced to sell; and remember that liquidity can vanish in a panic, so do not rely on being able to exit at the price you see today.

cards.definition: Borrowing from a broker to buy shares, using the shares as collateral. China's formal margin loans peaked at 2.27 trillion yuan in June 2015.
A broker's demand for more cash when the value of margined shares falls. Unmet calls lead to forced selling.
State-backed Chinese institutions that bought shares to support the market during the 2015 crash.
The daily rate China's central bank sets for the yuan, around which it is allowed to trade in a band.
Money rushing out of a country as investors and savers fear losses, as in China after August 2015.
When a trading halt is set too close, prices get pulled towards it as traders rush to sell before it triggers.

points: China's stock market rose about 150% in eleven months to June 2015, fuelled by state encouragement and record margin lending of 2.27 trillion yuan
The index fell 43% from June to August 2015 as margin calls forced selling, despite an estimated $200 billion or more of state buying and trading suspensions at more than half of listed companies
The 1.9% yuan devaluation on 11 August 2015 broke confidence in a managed currency and triggered capital flight
China's reserves fell from $3.99 trillion to under $3 trillion by January 2017 before tighter capital controls stopped the drain, a live example of the impossible trinity
India felt the shock through capital flight, with the Sensex falling 1,624 points on 24 August 2015, and the episode offers lessons for India's own leveraged retail trading boom
